title:
Sir Robert Peel created a new
                Conservative Party only to destroy it
author: Modern
content:
Sir Robert Peel created a new Conservative Party
only to destroy it. Discuss.

Author: Richard Parsons <
richard@hogarth.demon.co.uk
>

Comments:

It is certainly true that a superficial understanding of the facts surrounding
Peel in the 1830s and 1840s can lead to the conclusion that Peel was the
creator of a new Conservative Party and there are a number of ways in which
this can be argued. One of those is to say that Robert Peel modernised
the Conservative Party with regard to the social classes which it wanted
to appeal to in order to win votes. It can be argued that Peel, understanding
that those newly enfranchised by the Great Reform Act were potential Conservative
voters, had to shift the policies of the party in order to appeal to more
middle class voters. Evidence for this is the various issues on which Peel
seemed to be changing policy in order to attract the middle classes. One
way in which he did this was by making his party stand for moderate reform
as opposed to the previously reactionary history of the Conservative Party
under leaders such as Liverpool. On top of this it can be argued that Peel
shifted the policy of the Conservative party with regard to economics.
It has been suggested that the Tamworth Manifesto is evidence for saying
that Peel now wished to make the Conservative Party appeal to the conservative
interests of industry instead of just the land owning and the aristocratic
and that this was necessary for the Conservative recovery of the 1830s.
This is because surely in order for the Conservatives to recovery after
an extension of the franchise they must have appealed to middle class or
liberal ideas.

Similarly it has been argued that Peel created a new Conservative party
by altering the way that it was organised, modernising the structure of
the party in order to make it more competitive in the political system
of the future. Evidence for this is creation of the Carlton Club which
was a centre for Conservative actions during elections. Also the Conservatives
were ahead of their competitors in that they had the first political agent,
F. R. Bonham. Not only this but Peel was also apparently aware of the fact
that he must encourage potential Conservative voters to "register, register,
register" as he said in a public speech of the 1830s. Therefore it is this
enthusiasm for party organisation and the attempts of Peel to appeal to
middle class interests which have caused Peel to be labelled the creator
of a new Conservative Party in the 1830s.

However the a far stronger argument can be made for saying that Peel
did not create a new Conservative Party and that part of the proof of this
is the fact that the party elected in 1841 was essentially a party of traditional
Conservative ideals. The Tory MPs elected in 1841 had generally been committing
themselves to policies such as protection of agriculture, and defence of
the church, the union and the other constitutions. The Conservative candidates
had been using such arguments such as that the Conservatives were the party
which was most trust worthy and stable on issues such as law and order
and opposition to reform. The reason for the Conservative recovery was
not that it was the result of a shift of policy after the crushing defeat
of 1832 but that the odd circumstances of the reform crisis had now passed
and that a Conservative recovery was inevitable. Once the question of reform
was removed from the top of the political agenda then the middle class
in the country were bound to go back to voting Tory since many of them
believed  in these conservative values such as protectionism and defence
of the institutions. Anglicans who were strongly anti-Nonconformist and
those who were particularly anti-Irish were bound to see the Conservatives
as the people who most naturally represented their views. Therefore it
was not the case that the Conservatives were winning seats on a new policy,
but that Conservative support at grass roots in the country was essentially
voting Conservative because of the traditional policies and strengths of
Conservatism.

On top of this, the argument that Peel created a whole new organisation
for the Conservative Party can be countered by indicating the very nature
of politician that Peel was since it is clear that he was far more of a
traditionally minded Conservative regarding party structure even than most
of the other Conservatives. Although Peel saw the importance of registration
he was more of an eighteenth century politician interested in the loyalty
to the nation and the monarch than any party. In fact Peels personal part
in the modernisation of the Conservative Party was very limited indeed.
Party organisation was more of a consequence of growing Conservatism in
the country than a cause of it. In a political system where only about
a half of seats were contested it was still not necessary for the any real
party structure in order to win elections and had the Conservatives needed
to modernise its structure in order to be competitive, Peel would have
hardly been the best leader to do so.

In order to properly deal with the major split of the Conservative party
in 1846 over the repeal of the Corn Laws, it must be understood that the
seeds of the problem lay in the party which was elected in 1841. This was
because the Tories elected were essentially committed to traditionally
conservative policies whereas Peels priority was to shift the ground of
the party and he was expecting his party to follow him. The crisis was
therefore created by the fact that Peel wanted to introduce free trade
measures in the national interest whereas his party wanted to keep agricultural
protection in order to defend the aristocrats and land owners who were
to a great extent responsible for their election. Therefore the blame for
the destruction of the Conservative party must, to a large extent, lie
upon the shoulders of Peel because it was his limitations which led to
the major split. Peel belief was quite simple, that the Corn Laws were
unjust and not favourable to the majority of the country and therefore
should be removed. Because of the fact that he was more an eighteenth century
politician than his party, he believed that he, as the kings chief minister
should try to govern in the way which was best for the country as a whole.
On the other hand the rest of his party believed that their leader should
legislate in the interests of his party. This meant that the Corn Laws
were bound to be a problematic subject which was why Peel had been so quiet
about his opinions on the Corn Laws in the 1830s. However the blame can
be pushed further onto the head of Peel by understanding that it was Peels
inability to educate his party as to the advantages of free trade which
were so damaging. Had he been more charismatic he would have been able
to persuade his party of the good points of the Repeal. Therefore it was
a mixture of Peels concept of the relationship between government and
party compared with that of his party, and the his own inability to effectively
lead his party which led to the destruction of the Conservative Party in
1846.

To conclude, it is certainly true that Peel did try to change some of
the immediate policies of the Conservatives. However Peels own motives
were conservative at heart and the Tory MPs elected in 1841 were certainly
not the result of any new Conservatism but the consequence of the old Tory
ideals of deference and protection. In fact the fact that this party was
so traditional is shown by the fact that Peel destroyed by forcing the
Repeal of the Corn Laws. Had Peel truly created a new Conservative Party
of free trade and middle class ideals then it would have clearly supported
the Repeal. Not only that, but if Peel had been the new, modern politician
that the title suggests that he was, then he would have been more willing
to follow the dictates of his party than the interests of the country.
